documents.unit: Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: Syllabus Statements (AI Use statements section)
tiers: No Use of Generative AI Permitted
Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission
Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines
documents.summary: The teaching center page offers borrowed sample syllabus statements in three tiers of generative AI use and tells students to check each class's policy. A separate academic-integrity statement lists unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The AI section says the statements 'help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI, whose use might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline', and offers three sample tiers. The page sets no single rule for all courses, so the stance is delegates with tiers.

units.why: The AI section says the samples 'help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI', i.e. the institution supplies sample AI syllabus language. That is P110, not P63, since it gives wording rather than learning support.
units.resolution_why: Matched pair on the same passage. A coded P04 (the choice sits with each faculty member), B coded P110 (the institution supplies sample AI syllabus language). The source says the statements "are provided to help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI", which is the offer of sample wording, so P110 follows; the delegation of the choice is coded separately in the next unit as P04. Actor, phase and modality agree.
units.anchor: provided to help faculty communicate their policies regarding generative AI

units.why: The page says generative AI 'might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline and teaching methods their course uses'. No university rule is set; the decision follows discipline and course, so this is P04 (per instructor/course).
units.resolution_why: Matched pair. Both coded P04, informs, instructor. A set phase general, B before-course. The sentence is a principle ("might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline and teaching methods their course uses"), not a step in course design, so general. B's policy wording restates the source without addition and is kept.
units.anchor: whose use might or might not be appropriate depending on the academic discipline
units.policy: Whether generative AI use is appropriate depends on the academic discipline and the teaching methods of the course.

units.why: The page tells students to 'Make sure to check the specific policies for each of your classes', making them responsible for finding each course's AI rule. It is P78, not P10, because it is not about asking when unsure.
units.resolution_why: Both coders agree on all codes (P78, student, course-start, must). B's anchor includes the full sentence and is kept.
units.anchor: Make sure to check the specific policies for each of your classes.

units.why: The page groups its samples under three named headings, from no use to use under some circumstances to broader use. Named levels of permitted AI use are P05; I anchor the middle heading as the clearest span of the scheme.
units.resolution_why: Both coded P05, informs, instructor, before-course. Anchors differ (A the last heading, B the middle heading) but cover the same three headings. B's policy wording matches the source headings and is kept.
units.anchor: Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission
units.frag_end: Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines
units.policy: Sample AI statements are grouped in three tiers: No Use of Generative AI Permitted; Use of Generative AI Permitted Under Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission; Broader Use of Generative AI Permitted Within Guidelines.

units.why: Bryant sample: "AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage of work in this class" bans AI on all work, a default prohibition (P01).
units.resolution_why: Both agree: the Bryant sample "AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage of work in this class" is a default ban on all work, P01.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools are not permitted for any stage of work in this class.

units.why: The same sample says using these tools 'would be considered academically dishonest and a violation of Bryant's Academic Honesty Policy'. It classifies banned AI use as an integrity violation, which is P36.
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P36, student, when-misuse, informs, prohibit. B's policy wording is the more literal restatement of the sample and is kept.
units.anchor: your actions would be considered academically dishonest
units.policy: Using AI writing tools in the course is academically dishonest and violates the Academic Honesty Policy.

units.why: Princeton sample: "All work submitted in this course must be your own" requires students to own their submissions (P29); the AI ban in the next sentence is coded separately.
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P29, student, during-work, must. Topics merged.
units.anchor: All work submitted in this course must be your own

units.why: Princeton sample: "You may not ... make use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software" bans AI writing tools in the course; P01 rather than P19 because it bans use outright, not only submitting AI output.
units.resolution_why: Coders disagreed on type: A coded P01, B coded P19. The sentence "You may not engage in unauthorized collaboration or make use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software" bans using the tool at all, not only submitting its output, and the sample sits in the "No Use" tier as the course rule. P01 fits; P19 is about AI-produced submitted work and is narrower than this ban. Actor, phase, modality and unit_stance agree.
units.anchor: make use of ChatGPT or other AI composition software

units.why: Princeton sample opens with "Intellectual honesty is vital to an academic community and for my fair evaluation of your work", grounding the ban in honesty and fair evaluation (P95).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. "Intellectual honesty is vital to an academic community and for my fair evaluation of your work" is the sample's stated reason for its ban, a real rationale statement matching P95, so kept.
units.anchor: Intellectual honesty is vital to an academic community

units.why: The CU sample says students "will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used", so AI use is built into some course activities (P79).
units.resolution_why: Matched pair. Type (P79), actor, phase and unit_stance (require) agree. Modality differed: A informs, B must. The source says "you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used", a statement of what the course will do rather than an order in the sentence itself, so informs; must would strengthen the passage.
units.anchor: you will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used

units.why: 'You are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content ... that will end up in any student work' discourages AI without forbidding it, so P03.
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P03, student, during-work, should-not, restrict. B's normalized policy is faithful to the source and kept.
units.anchor: you are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content
units.frag_end: part of your evaluation in this course.
units.policy: Outside the activities that call for AI, students are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content (text, video, audio, images) that ends up in work that is evaluated.

units.why: "should clearly indicate what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI" requires marking AI-generated parts in a submission; P24 disclosure with each submission, not P27 since it is not about code.
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P24, student, during-work, should, permit. A's fit_note retained: the passage asks to separate student work from AI-generated parts, more specific than a general disclosure statement.
units.anchor: what work is the student's work and what part is generated by the AI
units.frag_start: Any student work submitted using AI tools
units.fit_note: Asks to separate student work from AI-generated parts within the work, more specific than a general disclosure statement.

units.why: "no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI" is a numeric cap on AI-generated content, which P16 lists as a percentage cap.
units.resolution_why: Type (P16), actor, phase and modality (should-not) agree. unit_stance differed: A restrict, B permit. "No more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI" is a cap that limits AI use, so restrict. Topic code-generation (both coders) replaced with permitted-uses because the sample is not about code; the fit_note records that P16 is the nearest type, not an exact one.
units.anchor: no more than 25% of the student work should be generated by AI
units.frag_start: In such cases, no more than 25%
units.fit_note: P16 is about AI-generated code; this cap applies to AI-generated content in student work in general (text, video, audio, images), not code.

units.why: "please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work" when confused: students ask before acting when unsure (P10).
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P10, student, during-work, should, neutral.
units.anchor: please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work

units.why: 'AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class' sets a permissive default for the course, so P02, with the condition of citation handled in the next unit.
units.resolution_why: Type, actor, phase and modality (may) agree. unit_stance differed: A encourage, B permit. "AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class, provided that you cite when and how you use the tool" welcomes AI under a citation condition, which is permit; encourage means AI is recommended.
units.anchor: AI Writing tools such as ChatGPT are welcome in this class
units.frag_end: cite when and how you use the tool.

units.why: 'Provided that you cite when and how you use the tool' makes citing AI use a condition of using it. This is disclosure with each submission (P24); 'when and how' goes a little beyond a bare statement.
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P24, student, during-work, must, permit. B's fit_note kept: "when and how" goes beyond a bare disclosure statement.
units.anchor: provided that you cite when and how you use the tool
units.frag_end: cite when and how you use the tool.
units.fit_note: Requires citing both when and how the tool was used, which is more detail than a bare disclosure statement.

units.why: "You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool" commits the instructor to supply citation examples; nearest type is P110 (sample language), so a fit note is added.
units.resolution_why: Coders disagreed on type and modality: A coded P110 (informs), B coded P25 (should). P110 covers sample language for instructors and P25 covers what a citation must contain; the passage "You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool in your writing" does neither (no elements named, and the examples go to students). Both flagged partial fit, so UNCOVERED rather than a stretched fit. Modality informs because the sentence states what will be provided, not an obligation. Actor instructor and phase course-start agree.
units.anchor: You will be provided with examples of how to cite your use of this tool
units.policy: Students are provided with examples of how to cite their use of the AI tool in their writing.
units.uncovered_note: The instructor gives students worked examples of how to cite AI use. (Merged coder fit notes: A, P110 fit only partly because these are examples given to students, not sample syllabus language for instructors; B, P25 fit only partly because the passage does not say which elements of a citation are required.)

units.why: Iowa sample: "work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original" requires submitted work to be genuinely the student's own (P29).
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P29, student, during-work, must, neutral.

units.why: The Iowa sample calls using an AI-content generator 'without proper attribution or authorization' 'a form of academic dishonesty'. It classifies unattributed or unauthorized AI use as dishonesty (P36).
units.resolution_why: Both agree on all codes (P36, student, when-misuse, must-not, restrict). B's policy is the verbatim sentence and is kept.
units.anchor: without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty
units.policy: Using an AI-content generator (such as ChatGPT) to complete coursework without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty.

units.why: Iowa sample: "please contact your instructor to discuss the issue" if unsure about plagiarism, i.e. ask the instructor when unsure (P10).
units.resolution_why: Both agree on P10, student, during-work, should. A's anchor kept because it includes the action (contact your instructor), whereas B's anchor ends at the condition.
units.anchor: please contact your instructor to discuss the issue

units.why: The integrity statement lists 'unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI)' beside cheating and plagiarism, so it classifies AI misuse as academic misconduct. It binds students, applies when misuse occurs, and fits P36 exactly.
units.resolution_why: Type (P36), actor and phase agree. Modality differed: A informs, B must-not; unit_stance A prohibit, B restrict. The sentence "Academic misconduct includes actions such as ... unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI)" binds students, and "unauthorized" means AI is allowed where authorized, so must-not and restrict. The same coding is used for the identical list item in the Student Code.
units.anchor: unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI)
units.policy: Academic misconduct includes unauthorized use of artificial intelligence (AI), alongside cheating, plagiarizing, fabricating false sources and unauthorized recording.

units.why: 'The student will be referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office' sets a procedural step once misconduct (which names unauthorized AI) occurs. P81 fits better than P37 because no concrete penalty is named; the grade effect is left to the instructor.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. "The student will be referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office" applies to the misconduct list that names unauthorized AI and sets the formal procedure step, P81 (no concrete penalty named, so not P37). B's policy also folded in "may have their grade impacted at the discretion of the instructor", a second rule; it is removed so the unit holds one rule. Kept.
units.anchor: referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office
units.frag_end: through the Dean of Students Office.
units.policy: A student who engages in academic misconduct, which includes unauthorized AI use, is referred to university disciplinary procedures through the Dean of Students Office.

units.why: The sentence points to University Regulations 3-2-203 and the Student Code for "the academic misconduct process", directing readers to the formal procedure (P81).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. "More information about the academic misconduct process can be found in University Regulations 3-2-203 and additional procedures outlined UNC's Student Code of Conduct" points to the formal process that governs AI misconduct cases, P81. A real pointer to the procedure, so kept as informs.
units.anchor: More information about the academic misconduct process can be found in University Regulations

documents.unit: Dean of Students, Student Code of Conduct (Bear Code)
documents.title: University Policies: Student Code of Conduct
documents.summary: The Student Code of Conduct names unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct and expects conduct outcome work to be free of generative AI. AI is allowed only when the instructor or a University Official permits it.
documents.stance_why: AI content is misconduct when "not permitted by the instructor or University Official", so AI is banned unless permitted; this is restrict, not prohibit, because permission can be granted.

units.why: The Code lists "Unauthorized use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)" as academic misconduct for AI content "not permitted by the instructor or University Official", classing unauthorized AI as misconduct (P36); permission is set by instructor or official.
units.resolution_why: Matched pair on the same passage. Both coded P36, student, when-misuse, must-not, restrict. A's policy states the full definition and is kept; B's shorter policy dropped the scope. The instructor/University Official permission condition is carried in this unit's policy; B's separate P04 unit on the same clause is not kept because the sentence only defines unauthorized use and does not itself hand a decision to instructors.
units.anchor: tools that are not permitted by the instructor or University
units.frag_start: The use or attempted use of
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI is academic misconduct: the use or attempted use of written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data generated by AI tools that are not permitted by the instructor or University Official

units.why: The definition covers "written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data" generated by AI, setting the scope of AI output covered (P61).
units.resolution_why: Matched on the overlapping passage but A coded P61 (scope: kinds of output covered), phase general, informs, actor all; B coded P04, general, must-not, actor student. The listing of "written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data" defines what the rule covers, which is scope, P61; the who-permits clause is in the P36 unit above. B's P04 is not kept. A's fit_note retained: it defines the kinds of output covered, not AI itself. Actor all because the scope definition applies to the whole code.
units.anchor: written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data
units.frag_start: The use or attempted use of
units.policy: The misconduct rule covers written content, images, tables, references, music or musical scores, or data generated by AI tools
units.fit_note: Defines the kinds of output covered, not AI itself.

units.why: Outcomes assigned in a conduct case 'are expected to be original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI' unless otherwise indicated. It bans AI from producing submitted work, here sanction assignments, so P19.
units.resolution_why: Matched pair on the same sentence. A coded P01, during-work, prohibit; B coded P19, when-misuse, restrict. These Outcomes are assignments given after a conduct finding, not graded course work, so P01 (default ban on graded work in a course) does not fit; they are work the student submits, so P19 fits. Phase when-misuse because Outcomes are sanctions after a finding. "Unless otherwise indicated" means the ban can be lifted, so restrict. B's policy is faithful to the source and kept.
units.anchor: original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI
units.policy: Unless otherwise indicated, Outcomes assigned under the Student Code are expected to be original work by the student and not produced with the assistance of generative AI.

units.why: "Outcomes are expected to be original work by the student" requires original student work; P29 for the ownership expectation, separate from the AI ban.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. "Outcomes are expected to be original work by the student" is a real ownership expectation in the same sentence as the AI limit, so kept as P29. Phase set to when-misuse for the same reason as the Outcomes unit above (conduct Outcomes are sanctions), where A had during-work.
units.anchor: Outcomes are expected to be original work by the student
units.frag_start: Unless otherwise indicated, Outcomes are expected

notes: Both documents are university-level (CETL syllabus statements page; Student Code of Conduct); no college or computing-unit AI policy found, course layer deferred. The CETL sample statements are borrowed from Bryant, Princeton, the Colorado system and Iowa and are offered as options, not UNC rules; they are coded as the page presents them. Dropped single-coder units: (1) A's "All external sources must be properly cited." (P24 with fit_note 'Generic citation duty for outcome work; AI is not named in this sentence'); (2) B's "Students are encouraged to review course syllabi to understand the expectations for each course in which they are enrolled" (P78). Neither sentence mentions AI and both are generic conduct-code lines. The grade-discretion clause in the syllabus misconduct paragraph ("may have their grade impacted at the discretion of the instructor") is generic to misconduct and not coded separately. Generic hearing, appeal and outcome procedures of the Code do not mention AI and were not coded.
